newsitem.title: USA: Gibson Greetings CEO wants to reinvent the card.
newsitem.headline: Gibson Greetings CEO wants to reinvent the card.

text.p: Gibson Greetings Inc. chief executive officer Frank O'Connell, after four months on the job, says he hopes to reinvent storm-tossed Gibson and the whole greeting card industry as well.
He wants consumers to have more choices, including competing brands of cards in supermarkets, drug stores and other retail stores which now primarily carry only one brand.
He wants to make it easier for time-harried shoppers to find the right card quickly, not spend precious minutes searching card racks.
"To me, the product has become progressively less relevant to the consumer," the former executive of a trading card firm and an athletic shoe maker said in a telephone interview Friday.
Greeting card sections in supermarkets and other stores "are 180 feet of boring product" that hasn't changed much in 40 years, he said.
The Cincinnati-based card maker had $388.9 million in sales in 1995 but is a distant third in market share.

Industry estimates are that privately held Hallmark Cards Inc, based in Kansas City, has about 42 percent of the card market and Cleveland-based American Greetings Corp. has about 36 percent. Gibson is estimated to have 6 percent to 8 percent, with much smaller companies splitting the rest.
Gibson, which O'Connell said has lost a bit of market share in the last few years, fired O'Connell's predecessor in February 1996.

Gibson had suffered 1994 derivatives losses then lost several key customers. Early this year, Gibson rebuffed a $290 million bid from rival American Greetings, citing antitrust concerns. Gibson has said it is no longer for sale.

After a 1994 loss, it returned to profitability in 1995 with earnings of $1.00 a share excluding results of an unprofitable division, which was sold. First Call said analysts expect it to earn $1.20-$1.25 a share in 1996 and $1.30-$1.40 a share in 1997.
Gibson's stock closed at $19.125 Friday on Nasdaq. It has risen from about $12 since O'Connell took the helm in August.
McDonald & Co analyst Jeffrey Stein said of O'Connell, "I wouldn't bet against him. He's got some very good ideas and I would bet he's going to succeed -- but not overnight."
O'Connell headed trading card manufacturer SkyBox
International, now part of Marvel Entertainment Group Inc., and also was president of athletic shoe maker Reebok International Ltd's Reebok Brands, North America.

O'Connell said he plans to revamp Gibson's product line, adding "a lot of new products at a high rate of speed" and incorporating new concepts to reach children, teenagers and "Generation X", the 20- to 30-something age group.

He also wants sell cards in music and video stores to reach young customers and sell cards featuring dogs and cats in pet food stores and pet departments of mass retailers. He said Gibson is also studying direct mail catalogues, on-line greetings and other possibilities, he said.
